 Notes from the Editors
 Daraxonrasib in Metastatic Pancreatic Cancer 
 It’s always exciting to see breakthroughs like the one described in this issue, the use of the RAS inhibitor daraxonrasib in metastatic pancreatic cancer. Of course, much of the excitement is because of the dramatic responses in a disease that has historically responded poorly to treatment. But, putting on my basic science hat, it’s great to see the fulfillment of a decades-long effort to find inhibitors of oncogenic KRAS proteins bearing oncogenic substitutions.
While we have a multitude of drugs that can target mutant forms of tyrosine kinases, for many years KRAS, a small GTP-binding protein, was thought to be undruggable. In the last few years, several compounds have made it into clinical trials, though these targeted relatively rare mutations. Because of their mechanism of action, daraxonrasib and related compounds could be broadly active, not just in pancreatic cancer but in the many tumor types associated with KRAS mutations. Hopefully, as we see the use of this and similar agents extended to other cancers, used in combination with other therapies, we will start to see longer survival times and, possibly, cures in other previously almost untreatable tumors.
Eric
